front: Angle of view — formula and the model it comes from
back: AOV = 2 · arctan( sensor_dimension / (2 · f) ). From the thin-lens PINHOLE model: sensor at the focal plane, lens as a point, half the sensor dimension over f is the tangent of the half-angle. Knowing the model tells you when it stops being true — fisheye uses a different projection entirely.

front: Field of view width — formula and derivation
back: W = D · w / f. From SIMILAR TRIANGLES: the scene at distance D and the sensor at distance f subtend the same angle, so W/D = w/f.

front: Why W = D·w/f is dimensionally sound despite mixing mm and ft
back: w/f is a ratio of two lengths in the SAME unit, so it is dimensionless. The millimetres cancel before the feet meet them. W inherits its unit entirely from D.

front: The inverse FOV formula — and why it matters more
back: f = D · w / W_required. A calculator gives coverage from a lens you already chose; a designer starts from a coverage REQUIREMENT and needs the lens. The requirement comes first, the hardware second.

front: Slant range — definition and formula
back: The true optical path from lens to target: sqrt( D² + (h_mount − h_target)² ). Use it instead of floor distance whenever mount height is a meaningful fraction of target distance.

front: Which cameras does ignoring slant range hurt most, and in which direction?
back: INDOOR cameras, and any camera where mount height is a meaningful fraction of distance. Ignoring it OVERSTATES pixel density, because it computes scene width at a shorter distance than the light actually travels. A camera 12 ft up looking 8 ft away has a 10.6 ft slant range — 33% further than the floor distance.

front: Depression angle — formula and why you care
back: arctan( (h_mount − h_target) / D ). A steep depression angle sees a forehead and a hat, not a face. Arithmetic can pass while the geometry has thrown the face away.

front: Pixel density — both forms
back: PPF = px / W, and the combined form PPF = px · f / (D · w). The second is the first with W = D·w/f substituted in. Use it when you do not care about the scene width itself.

front: Pixel density falls as 1/D. What falls as 1/D²?
back: ILLUMINANCE — the inverse square law for light. PPF is a LINEAR density (pixels per foot of a one-dimensional scene width), and scene width grows linearly with distance. Confusing them makes people believe doubling distance quarters usable resolution. It halves it.

front: D_max ∝ px · f — what trades against what?
back: Resolution and focal length trade against each other FOR RANGE. They do NOT trade against each other for COVERAGE. More pixels widen range at fixed coverage; a longer lens narrows coverage to buy range.

front: Maximum range for a DORI class — how to compute it
back: W_max = px / PPF_target, then D_max = W_max · f / w. Range scales LINEARLY with horizontal pixel count — 2688 → 3840 px is a 43% increase in range, not a doubling.

front: DORI values in pixels per metre and per foot
back: [STANDARD] IEC 62676-4: Detect 25, Observe 62.5, Recognise 125, Identify 250 px/m. [VERIFY current edition] Per foot in practice: 8 / 19 / 38 / 76.

front: Why is the per-foot DORI table not the exact metric conversion?
back: Exact conversions are 7.62 / 19.05 / 38.10 / 76.20. The table rounds to 8 / 19 / 38 / 76 — the values used in common practice — so your numbers match vendor datasheets and the room. Chasing 0.2 PPF of precision on a figure that is a minimum under GOOD conditions is false precision. The rounding is documented so you can undo it.

front: Rounding a computed focal length — which direction, and why?
back: ALWAYS ROUND UP to the next stocked size. Rounding down widens the field beyond the requirement and REDUCES pixel density — you fail the requirement you just computed. Then re-verify that the narrower field still covers what you need.

front: Three things pixel density does not tell you
back: (1) Whether there is any light — PPF is geometric and identical at noon and 2 a.m. (2) Whether the image is sharp — MTF, focus error, motion blur and compression all destroy detail the geometry says is there. (3) Whether the face is pointed at the camera. Geometric PPF is NECESSARY, never SUFFICIENT.

front: Where does a bitrate figure legitimately come from? (ranked)
back: (1) A MEASURED stream from a pilot of the actual camera in the actual scene. (2) The manufacturer datasheet for that model, codec and profile. (3) A vendor bandwidth calculator. (4) A generic reference table [PRACTICE] — a starting point you must caveat.

front: Why is frame-rate scaling sub-linear?
back: (1) I-frames and container overhead do not scale with frame rate — a fixed cost per GOP stays fixed. (2) Inter-frame prediction gets LESS efficient at low frame rates, because successive frames differ more, so each P-frame carries more residual. Model: bitrate × (to_fps/from_fps)^0.7 [PRACTICE].

front: Order of operations: frame-rate scaling and codec factor
back: Scale for frame rate FIRST, then apply the codec factor. 10 Mbps at 30→15 fps: 10 × 0.5^0.7 = 6.1557 Mbps H.264, × 0.5 = 3.0779 Mbps H.265.

front: Why does a documented modelling choice beat an undocumented one?
back: A documented choice can be challenged, tested, and replaced. An undocumented one gets inherited silently by everyone downstream and becomes indistinguishable from a fact.

front: Storage is sized on average bandwidth, links on peak. Why?
back: Storage ACCUMULATES over time, so it integrates the average. A link must carry whatever arrives right now, so it must survive the peak. And peaks CORRELATE — one vehicle triggers the gate, two fence cameras and a dock camera within seconds — so the statistical smoothing you hoped for evaporates exactly when you need it.

front: A motion duty cycle below 1.0 — risk or saving?
back: A RISK TO BE NAMED, not a saving to be booked. It assumes motion detection fires on every event that matters. Motion recording that misses the event produces nothing. Book it as a saving and you have quietly transferred a technical risk to the owner without telling them.

front: GB/day from a bitrate — the four steps
back: Mbps × 3600 s/h × hours ÷ 8 (bits→bytes) ÷ 1000 (MB→GB). Example: 5.0 Mbps × 3600 × 24 = 432,000 megabits → 54,000 megabytes → 54.0 GB/day.

front: Converting decimal megabytes to GiB — the divisor
back: Divide by 2³⁰/10⁶ = 1073.741824, NOT by 1024. A bitrate is DECIMAL, so the intermediate megabytes are 10⁶ bytes. Dividing by 1024 reports roughly half the true gap — the classic error, and one psec.video actually contained until Module 32 was written.

front: The decimal/binary gap — the two figures to remember
back: GB → GiB: 6.868%. TB → TiB: 9.051%. The TB figure applies the mismatch twice (once at GB, once at TB) while GiB → TiB is a clean 1024, because both are already binary.

front: Why the decimal/binary gap matters commercially
back: The client buys disk labelled in decimal TB and their OS reports capacity in TiB. A 22 TB array shows as roughly 20 TiB. If nobody explains the 9% in advance, it gets discovered as a shortfall at handover.

front: How to present a storage figure to a client
back: As a RANGE with the point estimate inside it, plus a commitment to close it: we are sizing at X TB, the true figure depends on scene activity and could land between A and B, so we are specifying expansion bays and will measure real bitrate in week one. Default range multipliers 0.7× to 1.6× [PRACTICE].

front: Two vendors' bandwidth calculators disagree by 2× on the same camera. Who is wrong?
back: Neither, necessarily. Bitrate at design time depends on scene content, motion, noise, lighting, codec implementation and encoder tuning — none of which anyone knows yet. A 2× spread reflects GENUINE UNCERTAINTY. The skill is not computing a number; it is computing a number and communicating how much you trust it.

front: The inverse storage problem — and why you will be asked it
back: How many days does the storage they ALREADY OWN buy? TB_available ÷ TB_per_day. It is the most common retrofit question and the answer is usually far worse than the client believes — and they may have told an auditor otherwise.

front: RAID efficiency by level
back: RAID 0: 1.0. RAID 1 and 10: 0.5. RAID 5: (n−1)/n. RAID 6: (n−2)/n. Raw capacity needed = usable ÷ efficiency.

front: What RAID protects against — and what it does not
back: Protects: the loss of n disks in a group (1 for RAID 5, 2 for RAID 6) without data loss or downtime. Does NOT protect against: controller failure, chassis loss, fire, water, theft of the recorder, ransomware, deletion, or a config error that stopped recording. It is not a backup. During a rebuild the array is slower and less redundant.

front: PSE power vs PD power
back: PSE = what the switch port must SOURCE. PD = what the device may DRAW. Datasheets quote PD; you budget against PSE. The difference is the worst-case cable loss the standard allows.

front: PoE class allocations [STANDARD] 802.3af/at/bt
back: af (Type 1): 15.4 PSE / 12.95 PD. at (Type 2, PoE+): 30.0 / 25.5. bt Type 3: 60.0 / 51.0. bt Type 4: 90.0 / 71.3. All watts. [VERIFY current edition]

front: Why budget a switch on class allocation rather than datasheet draw?
back: Many switches allocate power by the CLASS the device negotiates, not by what it consumes — so a 6 W camera that classifies as Type 2 can hold 30 W of the budget hostage. Whether your switch does static or dynamic allocation is a per-model question. [VERIFY per switch datasheet] Class is the conservative answer.

front: The four independent ways a PoE switch design fails
back: (1) Port count exceeded. (2) Power budget exceeded. (3) Insufficient spare ports against the growth policy. (4) Budget tight — over ~80% utilised, so the NEXT device fails. They are INDEPENDENT: adding ports does not add watts.

front: Why is quoting spare PORTS to a client misleading?
back: Because it names the constraint that is probably not binding. A switch can have 14 empty ports and power for only 2 more outdoor cameras. Quote the BINDING constraint, in the units the client thinks in — cameras, not watts. Otherwise someone makes a commitment you cannot keep.

front: Why does PoE not need a voltage-drop calculation?
back: Because the standard solved it. A PSE sources 44–57 V into a link whose resistance is bounded by the cable spec and whose length is bounded to 100 m, and the PD accepts the whole range. The PSE-to-PD gap (15.4 vs 12.95, 30.0 vs 25.5) IS the cable loss allowance, already paid for.

front: When does the PoE protection end?
back: The moment you leave PoE. A 12 V DC lock on copper you chose, at a length you chose, has nothing bounding the drop except you.

front: Voltage drop — the working formula and its derivation
back: Vd = 2 · K · I · L / CM. Step 1: Ohm's law V = I·R. Step 2: R = K · L_total / CM. Step 3: round trip means L_total = 2L.

front: The factor of 2 in the voltage drop formula
back: The ROUND TRIP. Current leaves on one conductor and returns on the other, and both have resistance. Forgetting it halves your answer and is the single most common error in this calculation.

front: What is a circular mil?
back: The area of a circle one thousandth of an inch in diameter. Area in circular mils = (diameter in mils)², with no π. It exists precisely to make the voltage drop formula arithmetic instead of geometry.

front: Why K = 12.9 rather than a room-temperature value?
back: 12.9 Ω·cmil/ft is copper at ~75 °C. Resistance RISES with temperature, so a calculation at 20 °C understates drop on a loaded circuit in a hot ceiling. The warm-conductor value is the conservative choice — and it is why marginal circuits fail in the afternoon.

front: An access-controlled door releases reliably at 7 a.m. and intermittently by 3 p.m. First hypothesis?
back: VOLTAGE DROP with a marginal margin. Copper resistance rises with temperature, so a ceiling that is cool in the morning and warm by mid-afternoon pushes a circuit sitting 0.1 V above minimum below it. Measure voltage AT THE LOCK WHILE ENERGISED, and measure actual current draw.

front: Circular mils by AWG (the sizes that matter in security work)
Maximum run length — the inverted formula
back: L_max = (V_supply − V_min) · CM / (2 · K · I). V_min comes from the DEVICE datasheet, not a rule of thumb.

front: Which supply voltage do you calculate against?
back: The LOW end, not the nominal. A battery-backed supply sags toward the bottom of its range on standby — calculate at 12.0 V (or lower) rather than 13.8 V, then re-check at the end-of-standby sag. The circuit has to work during the outage, which is when nobody is available to diagnose it.

front: Multi-segment voltage drop — how to size it correctly
back: Sum the drops: Vd_total = Σ (2·K·I·L / CM) over every segment. To SIZE, work backwards from the load: the device needs V_min, the last segment takes X volts, so the previous segment must deliver V_min + X. Sizing any single segment in isolation is how you specify the conductor that fails.

front: Why 'always check the power transfer' is a defect, not a rule
back: Because which segment dominates depends entirely on L/CM for each. A long home run in 18 AWG can be 92% of the total drop with the 8 ft transfer at 8%; a short home run with a very thin transfer reverses it. COMPUTE BOTH, every time. The habit is the defect.

front: Three things that fix voltage drop — and what does not
back: Fix: bigger conductor, shorter run (move the supply closer), or higher supply voltage (same power at half the current halves the drop). Does NOT fix: a bigger power supply. The supply is not the problem; the copper is.

front: Battery amp-hours — the sizing formula
back: Ah = (I_standby × H_standby + I_alarm × H_alarm) × derate × aging. Defaults: derate 1.25, aging 1.25 [PRACTICE].

front: Why multiply the derate and aging factors instead of adding?
back: They describe INDEPENDENT reductions in delivered capacity: aging removes a fraction of what remains after the discharge derate, not a fraction of the original. 1.25 × 1.25 = 1.5625, not 1.5. Adding under-sizes by 4.167%.

front: What the discharge derate accounts for
back: Lead-acid delivers less than rated capacity at higher discharge rates and lower temperatures (Peukert effect), and you should not fully discharge it.

front: What the aging factor accounts for
back: Capacity loss over service life. Sizing a battery to exactly meet the requirement on day one means it fails to meet it in year two.

front: Peak current governs ___; standby current governs ___
back: Peak (alarm) current governs the POWER SUPPLY. Standby current governs the BATTERY. The most commonly reversed pair in low-voltage design.

front: Why do peak and standby current govern different things?
back: They answer different questions. The supply must deliver the worst INSTANTANEOUS demand without its output collapsing — a POWER question. The battery must deliver ENERGY OVER TIME, and the worst instant lasts seconds, so it barely touches amp-hours.

front: How much does the alarm component contribute to a battery?
back: Typically under 10%. Example: 4.5 A for 5 minutes is 0.37 Ah against a 5.17 Ah raw total — 7%. The same 4.5 A is 100% of the supply selection. Same two numbers, opposite roles.

front: Why does fail-secure hardware barely touch the battery?
back: Fail-secure locks are DE-ENERGISED at rest and draw only when released. They can be 15% of standby current and 60% of alarm current on the same panel.

front: Runtime estimate — formula and the usable fraction
back: runtime_h = Ah × usable_fraction / load_A, usable_fraction ≈ 0.8. You should not discharge sealed lead-acid to zero; the honest capacity is what you can take out without destroying the asset. First-order only — real runtime depends on rate, temperature and age.

front: Sizing calculation vs runtime check — which do you trust?
back: The SIZING calculation. Runtime is a sanity test, not a selection tool: a 7 Ah battery shows 4.67 h against a 4 h requirement and still fails, because that figure has been neither derated nor aged.

front: The current missing from power_supply_sizing
back: BATTERY CHARGING CURRENT. It comes from the POWER SUPPLY datasheet (the charger's rated output), not the battery's, and must be added to design current before selection. [VERIFY per datasheet]

front: Battery standby durations — who decides?
back: [CODE][VERIFY] NOT you. NFPA 72 sets fire alarm secondary power; UL 294 addresses access control standby; the adopted edition and the AHJ decide. The defaults in psec are engineering practice, not a compliance determination. Sizing perfectly against the wrong duration is still wrong.

front: When a computed result changes the CATEGORY of the problem
back: Jumping from 4 h to 24 h standby takes a battery from 8 Ah to 46 Ah, which changes the ENCLOSURE (does not fit a standard can), the CHARGING TIME (52 Ah at 1 A takes ~2 days), and adds charging current to the supply load. The calculator answers the energy question and hands you three it cannot answer. Notice when that happens.

front: The four quantities in timely detection
back: T_T total task time (start of the sequence to completing the act at the asset). T_D time to detection AND ASSESSMENT. T_A adversary time remaining after detection = T_T − T_D. T_R response force time.

front: The timeliness inequality
back: T_D + T_R < T_T, equivalently T_A > T_R. With a confidence margin: T_A − T_R > margin.

front: Why is assessment time added to T_D?
back: Because an unassessed alarm has not initiated a response. Detection that nobody has confirmed and acted on has not started the response clock. It is the cheapest term in the inequality to improve and the one nobody looks at.

front: Why is detection modelled at task COMPLETION rather than task start?
back: Because it is the CONSERVATIVE choice. A door contact reports when the door opens, not when the adversary begins working on it. Modelling detection at task start would credit you with time you do not have.

front: Required detection point — formula and what to do with it
back: T_D_max = T_T − T_R − margin. Walk the path, find which task the adversary is executing at that elapsed time, and place detection at or before it. This is how a detection layer gets located BY CALCULATION instead of by habit.

front: Remember: T_D_max is a budget for detection PLUS assessment
back: A 140 s required detection point with a 45 s assessment delay means the SENSOR must fire by 95 s. Assessment eats the budget before any sensor has been chosen. This is the most commonly missed step in the whole model.

front: The three verdicts, and why marginal is treated as not timely
back: TIMELY (margin exceeds the required confidence margin), MARGINAL (margin positive but below it), NOT TIMELY (margin ≤ 0). Marginal counts as not timely because landing exactly on your confidence margin means you have consumed the entire allowance for being wrong. A tool answering a question about whether people get hurt should round toward the uncomfortable answer.

front: Why does adding delay before the detection point buy nothing?
back: Because T_A = T_T − T_D, and delay added before detection increases BOTH by the same amount. T_A is unchanged and the verdict does not move. Delay only counts if it sits AFTER the detection point on the path.

front: The four intervention levers
back: (1) Detect earlier. (2) Add delay AFTER the detection point. (3) Reduce response time — usually the dominant term and usually an OWNER decision. (4) Reduce the CONSEQUENCE. The fourth is not a term in the inequality, which is exactly why nobody proposes it.

front: Why include a lever that is not in the equation?
back: Because reducing the consequence — move, reduce, or eliminate the asset — is frequently the cheapest option available, and it is the ONLY lever that still helps after the system has failed. The other three change the probability of interruption; this one changes what a failure costs.

front: A required detection point comes out NEGATIVE. What does it mean?
back: Timeliness would require detecting the adversary before they begin. NO placement of detection anywhere on this path can succeed — the detection lever is EXHAUSTED, not merely expensive. Even instantaneous detection at the property line leaves less time than the response needs.

front: What should a calculator return for a negative detection point?
back: An explicit NOT ACHIEVABLE verdict in words, with the arithmetic, redirecting to response time or consequence reduction. 'Move detection to −240 s' is arithmetically true and operationally meaningless — and someone will try to build it.

front: The five limits of the timely-detection model
back: (1) One path — the adversary picks the weakest, not the one you analysed. (2) No detection PROBABILITY term; P_D is assumed 1.0. (3) Task delays are estimates, often illustrative rather than tested. (4) Response time is usually a contract figure, never measured. (5) It says nothing about what the responder does on arrival.

front: Which limit of the path model is most dangerous, and why?
back: The assumed P_D of 1.0. A fence sensor with a real P_D of 0.6, or a door contact defeated with a magnet, silently invalidates the entire calculation while every number in the output stays the same. Nothing in the result hints that the assumption was made.

front: Where would you spend the first dollar reducing path-model uncertainty?
back: On TESTED PENETRATION DATA for the actual construction. It is cheap, one-time, and every other number in the analysis is downstream of it. Reducing uncertainty at the root beats padding margins at the leaves.

front: Continuous vs binary uncertainty — the different treatments
back: Uncertainty in a CONTINUOUS output (storage) can be CARRIED: present a range, buy expandable hardware, measure later. Uncertainty in a BINARY output (timely / not timely) must be RETIRED: get real data or raise the margin, because 'the system is 60% likely to be timely' is not something a client can act on.

front: Why derive a calculation you already have working code for?
back: (1) A calculator you cannot derive is a calculator you cannot DEBUG — when two tools disagree by 30%, only the derivation says which is wrong. (2) The design direction is the INVERSE, and calculators run forwards. (3) Assumptions live in the derivation, not the output.

front: The cheapest defect detector in engineering
back: DIMENSIONAL ANALYSIS. Track your units at every step. The one real defect found while writing Module 32 was a decimal megabyte divided by 1024 — code that had been written, reviewed and tested, caught only by working the units by hand.

front: A test fails after you change a formula. What do you do?
back: REDO THE HAND CALCULATION. Do not change the test. The test encodes the derivation; if it disagrees with your new formula, one of them is wrong and it is not automatically the test.
